### PP_Recruiting: not now, and what would change that

Assessed 2026-09-19 against the 009 workbook and the 09-16 validation run. **Nothing
here is worth building today.** Recording it so it does not get re-litigated.

The screening engine itself is out of scope permanently: it compares percentiles to
thresholds (75th percentile, 0.375 elite share, Impact 90+), which is the exact thing
the jaggedness page says Jev is unreliable at. Its real weakness is calibration, not
judgment quality. The 09-16 validation ran low by 0.77 tiers on average, 1.25 against
Power Four, and caught 5 of 15 defensive players. That is fixed by more graded
validation players and code, not by a different model.

Two candidates that looked like fits and are not:

- **Player entity resolution.** Collapses to a code join. Telemetry carries a stable
  `PlayerId`, and `load_leaderboard.py` already joins Player Traits to Advanced Stats
  on it. The one open cross-source question (Jordan Church) is a single name against
  the recap list, and 30 of 30 transfers already matched by hand. One player is not a
  pattern.
- **Role assignment (WR/SLOT, END/JACK, CB/STAR).** The live blocker on deliverable
  010, so this was the one worth wanting. Inputs are alignment codes (OWR/SWR, ILB/OLB,
  OCB/SCB), already deterministic in both scripts, plus percentiles. Nothing
  text-shaped to decide on.

**The one real fit is text to features, and it has no input corpus.** It aims straight
at the weakest spot, defense, where percentile data is thinnest and film language is
richest. But pre-portal FCS and G6 players at week 5 to 6 have Telemetry percentiles
and nothing else. **Trigger: revisit when scouting text exists** — either the personnel
staff member starts writing evals on REVIEW rows (the 30 to 50 names per position he
asked for), or players hit the portal and recruiting services publish on them. Shape
when that day comes: not "is this a good corner," but 20 to 30 independent narrow
questions per note (*Noul: the note describes him redirecting without losing speed.
Noul: the note describes him losing leverage against bigger blockers. Score 1 to 5: how
much of this note is about his hands.*) in one request, weights in our code.

Two constraints that narrow it further whenever it is revisited:

- **Jev cannot live in the workbook.** The staff member runs the weekly refresh himself
  in Excel and Power Query. Any Jev step is Eric-run preprocessing, so it must be
  batch-once like the baseline load, or a standing Monday job. That rules out most of
  what is otherwise tempting, and the weekly refresh is the one piece someone else runs
  without Eric — a network call on that path is a straight downgrade.
- **Tier A here is about the wrong risk.** These are public college players, not Baylor
  athletes, so the health-data tiers do not bind. But Telemetry grades are licensed
  vendor data, and sending 8,761 rows to `api.typesafe.ai` is a question under
  **Telemetry's own terms on third-party processing**. Settle that before any of this,
  including anything small.

## What this unlocks that we cannot do today

Four of these are genuinely new capability, not a cheaper version of something we have.

**1. Free text becomes model features.** The autoresearch cookbook turns 2,000 wine
tasting notes into 67 numeric columns and trains CatBoost on them. Held-out RMSE went
from 3.09 (predict the mean) to 2.47 (word counts) to 2.15 (just ask Jev for the score)
to **1.77** (38 decomposed feature questions). The decomposition beat asking directly,
which is the whole thesis. Our equivalent: coach notes, wellness comments, RTP
narrative, and scouting text become inputs to a model instead of prose nobody scores.
Start on CFB scouting or public text, which is tier A. Athlete narrative is tier B or C
and waits.

**2. ~~Athlete ID reconciliation without a threshold to fit.~~ WITHDRAWN 2026-09-20 —
measured, and there is no problem here to solve.** ~~We have the same name spelled four
ways across Catapult, VALD, Perch, S2, and the roster, and today that is
hand-matching.~~ The entity-alignment recipe makes the three Score levels *be* the three
actions (leave unlinked, send to a curator, merge), so there is no number to tune, and
rides three Nouls along in the same request to tell the curator which field disagrees.
On 450 pairs it settled 89% automatically and queued 11%. Athlete names are PII, so
this is tier B and needs a de-identified key mapping first.

> **What the measurement found** (`athlete_matching/measure_residue.py`, full write-up
> in `ATHLETE_KEY_MAPPING.md`):
>
> - The premise above is **false**. The name is not "spelled four ways": of the 300
>   athletes that found any counterpart above 80, **287 settle on exact normalised
>   string equality**, every one scoring 100, with nothing in the 95–99 band. The
>   residue is **13 pairs**. (Settled means string-equal, not confirmed same person —
>   see the doc's caveats; with no DOB that gap is a missing attribute, not a
>   judgment a model could supply.)
> - The 89%/11% figure quoted here is from the cookbook's own dataset, not ours.
>   Measured on Baylor's data the split is 96%/4%, and the 96% needs no model —
>   `lower()`, strip punctuation, drop suffixes, collapse initials, join.
> - The tier-B blocker is also moot twice over: Eric cleared Option C on 2026-09-20,
>   and there is nothing left worth sending anyway.
>
> This entry stays visible rather than being deleted, because the reasoning that put
> it at #2 was sound and only an actual measurement moved it. The lesson worth keeping
> is that it was ranked on an assumed data condition nobody had checked — the same way
> the PP_Recruiting entity-resolution case was proposed before a `grep` killed it.

**3. Ask a policy document a plain question.** Tag each line with an ID, send one
Choice over the line IDs plus one Noul asking whether the document answers at all. The
Noul is what stops it from confidently pointing at the closest wrong line: on a
question the GitHub ToS does not answer, the top line still scored 0.86 while `exists`
read 0.14. Point it at the NCAA charter and Baylor policy. Cap is 255 lines per request; longer documents need a two-stage narrowing.

**4. A cheap verifier in front of expensive output.** This is the one I would not have
predicted. Every deliverable that leaves this machine (status report, Research in 5
deck, evidence brief) can be screened per-claim before it goes out, at roughly $0.00005
a call. The sde_cascade rules for a good verifier signal: one narrow grounded yes/no
per field, framed so *true* means escalate, aggregated with `max` so one confident red
flag survives instead of being averaged into silence.

## Where not to use it

- **Numeric verification on its own.** Correcting my 09-19 chat answer: the citation
  pipeline does apply to the TOS brief, but the part that catches a misquoted number is
  the **code string-match in step 1**, not Jev. Jev's Choice catches "this section says
  the opposite of the claim" (it flagged one at 0.99 confidence). Use both, and do not
  ask Jev whether 3.2 equals 3.2.
- **Date and window arithmetic.** Kickoff-time math in the sleep scheduler, GPS pull
  windows, availability windows. Extract parts, compute in code.
- **Anything that needs prose out.** It does not generate. Output is free because there
  is none.
- **Any per-athlete GPS, force plate, DEXA, or S2 record**, until Baylor IT says
  otherwise. Our own smoke test already posted a hamstring-tightness note to
  `api.typesafe.ai`. It was synthetic, and it shows how small the slip is.
- **As a security boundary.** The injection Noul is a filter, not a gate. Treat every
  passage that reaches a prompt as untrusted regardless of its score.

## Sequence

**First: the skill router.** It pays off across all 23 projects rather than one, and the
fit question I flagged on 09-19 is now resolved: 182 skills render to 16,089 characters,
about 4k tokens, so our ~155 fit inside the 32k budget with room to spare. Measured on
488 requests against Haiku 4.5, wrong skill loads fell 16.8% to 7.3% and needless loads
9.8% to 4.0%. It fixed 37 requests and broke 7.

Design constraints that are not optional here:

- It runs as a `UserPromptSubmit` hook, which means a network call on **every** prompt.
  Our memsearch hook is currently failing with `ETIMEDOUT` 8x consecutively. Same
  fragility class.
- Therefore: hard timeout around 2 seconds, **fail open** (no suggestion, never a
  blocked prompt), and no retries in the hot path.
- Use the cookbook's exact wording, including "Ignore this if it does not fit what the
  user actually asked for." Pushing harder wins compliance on wrong suggestions too.
- Patch both `.claude/hooks/` and `.codex/hooks/`, and run it under the shell the
  MSYS-stall fix settled on, not Git Bash.

**Next two, in order:** Zotero backlog classification with confidence backoff (tier A,
small, and the 1,018-papers-for-$0.08 demo is literally the same job), then the
deliverable verifier on the status report and Research in 5.

## Re-ranked 2026-09-20, after five items were resolved

All three of the original sequence shipped. Five of fourteen rows are now closed:
`skill_suggestion` (live), `classification_using_confidence` (1,418 records),
`citation_check` (live and gating, 6 of 6 after the apparatus strip),
`entity_alignment` (**withdrawn**, measured) and PP_Recruiting screening (**rejected**).

### The rule this project earned, stated as a gate rather than a story

Every item that was measured moved, and every one moved *down*. Entity alignment was
ranked second and was withdrawn. PP_Recruiting offered two obvious fits that both
collapsed into code. The Zotero renames were recommended skip. `AUTO_ACCEPT` came in
at the cookbook's 0.90 and measured to 0.80; the Zotero cutoff came in at 0.90 and
measured to 0.50. That is not bad luck, it is a missing gate. **Build only where all
three hold:**

1. **The answer is genuinely fuzzy** — not a join, not a threshold, not a lookup.
2. **Something already consumes the answer.** No consumer, no build. This is the
   Zotero-renames test.
3. **A code baseline was measured first.** If deterministic code gets most of the way,
   the model is decoration.

Each withdrawn item failed a *different* one of these, which is why no single check
would have caught them. Entity alignment failed (1) — exact string equality settled
287 of 300 and fuzzy matching contributed zero settled pairs. The Zotero renames
failed (2). The prose-number work nearly failed (3) and was saved only because the
band was measured before and after.

### Answer-key audit: a required step in every pre-registered test (added 2026-09-26)

Three measurements found a bad answer key, not a bad model: the surgery count (17 by
regex, 22 under blind labels), the Evidence Library tags (the reviewed labels sided
with Jev on 5 of 8 rules-picks), and the spring notes (role words the labels missed).
The "Just Ask Jev" paper (arXiv 2609.29429) reports the same on three public
benchmarks. So every pre-registration now carries this step, written down before the
first call:

1. **Pull the confident disagreements.** Every item where Jev's probability clears the
   pre-registered confidence cut and its answer differs from the label. Fix the cut
   in the pre-registration, not after seeing results.
2. **Eric judges them blind.** Shuffle, hide which side said what, show only the input
   and the two answers. He marks label right, Jev right, or unclear.
3. **Report both scores.** The pre-registered score on the original labels decides
   pass or fail, and the bar never moves. The audited score is reported next to it,
   and the count of labels changed is a finding in its own right.
4. **Cap the audit.** At most 20 items. If there are more than 20 confident
   disagreements, audit a random 20 and report the rate. More than that is a label
   problem worth its own write-up.

What this is not: a way to rescue a failed test. A test that fails on the original
labels and passes on the audited ones is reported as FAIL, with the audit as the reason
to re-run against fresh labels.

> **ANSWERED 2026-09-20 — `sde_cascade` is a CODE LINTER, not a Jev build.** The

> in `docs/SDE_CASCADE_SCOPING.md`; code in `sde_cascade/inventory.py`.
>
> **Stated precisely, because the margin is narrower than the headline:** the
> decision holds on the measured share and under either adversarial bound alone, on
> every seed. Stacking *both* bounds at once — assume every ambiguous statement is

> non-path quoted token — gives 21.6–29.9%, which crosses 25% on 2 of 4 seeds. Code
> linter is the right call; "not a close call" is not.
>
> The best single check is *does every backticked path still resolve?*, and it
> covers **39.3%** of code claims — not the 84.9% the shape table suggests, which
> counts any quoted token. The prototype's real cost is false alarms, not coverage:
> the unresolved rate walked from 43% to 24% **without finding one extra file**,
> purely by learning that `~/DEV/` is the Mac layout, that cross-repo references are
> the common case, and that the SecondBrain vault is Mac-only. Fourth item
> measurement has moved down the map.

**1. `sde_cascade` — but scoped, and the scoping is the deliverable.**
The target surface is real and large: **126 `STATUS.md` files and 79 handoffs** in
`~/DEV`. The failure is live — on 2026-09-20 three documents asserted the running
header was stripped when it removed nothing, and this very file's sibling asserted
the citation band "is the bibliography", which aimed the session's top-priority task
one layer too shallow.

But "verify our state claims" is a category, not a build, and as a category it has
exactly the smell that got entity alignment withdrawn. Sort the claims first:

| claim shape | example from 09-20 | who checks it |
|---|---|---|
| a date, count, path, or "does X exist" | "`perch.duckdb` last written 2026-04-30" | **code** — `stat`, `git`, a byte count |
| a step's effect | "the running header is stripped" | **code** — assert `chars_removed > 0` |
| prose about what a linked document says | "PRs #7 and #8 are not merged"; "`run_pipeline.py` exists" | **Jev** — this is `citation_check`'s exact shape |
| a causal claim | "the band *is* the bibliography" | **neither** — needs a controlled measurement |

So the honest first step is not code, it is an **inventory**: take ten handoffs,
classify every claim into those four rows, and count. If the Jev-shaped row is under
about a quarter, `sde_cascade` is a code linter that needs no model, and should be
built as one. Same pattern as `measure_residue.py` — measure the residue, let the
number decide. **Do that inventory before writing any Jev call.**

memsearch is rung L1 of the retrieval ladder in `memory-write`, hit on every "did we
already…?", against a haystack of 126 STATUS files, 79 handoffs, ~230 compiled
articles and the daily logs. One Noul per query-candidate pair, tier A, small.

Pre-register the test before building: pull **ten real past questions** from the
transcripts, record whether the right answer is in the current top-5, and only build
if it is not. If the hit rate is already 9 of 10, reranking buys nothing and this is
the Zotero-renames trap wearing a different hat.

**3. `composite-scoring` — possible, with the caveat stated up front.**
The consumer is real (`project-triage/slate.py`, with tests; the slate is capped at 5

call by design rather than a bottleneck. Either find a bigger ranking surface (the
full project registry, not the slate) or accept it as low-value and skip it. Do not
run the five-item comparison and treat agreement as validation.

## Drive triage, the tenth measurement (scored 2026-09-28): FAIL, used anyway

Pre-registration: `docs/DRIVE_TRIAGE_PREREG.md`. Results: `drive_triage/results.md`.

| Bar | Needed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Confident (p >= 0.50) | 60% of 200 | 166/200 (83%): pass |
| Domain accuracy, confident answers | 90% | 127/166 (76.5%): **fail** |
| Jev vs Haiku, same subset | Jev >= Haiku | 127 vs 108: pass |

- **Jev won every comparison and still missed the absolute bar.** On all 200 it beat Haiku on
  domain (74.5% vs 66.0%) and topic (63.5% vs 52.0%). Codex (200/200) tied it on domain
  (148 vs 149) but was worse on the unclassified half (75 vs 81) and has no confidence signal.
- **Where it held up:** the files the keyword rules could not place, which is the population
  Flint actually needs. There Jev's confident answers were right on 85.2% (69/81). On files the
  rules had already placed, it was right on only 68.2%.
- **What hurt:** the state. 87 of 200 files had no first-page text (video, scans, empty Drive
  entries). A file name and a folder cannot carry a 90% bar.
- **Decision (Eric, 2026-09-28):** Jev does Flint's pass, with Eric's shortlist approval kept
  as the check. The verdict stays FAIL, and this is not a rescue under the audit rule.

**The lesson for the next pre-registration.** The fail branch said "the best comparator does
the pass". It never said what happens when the model fails its bar but beats every
comparator. That left a decision to be made after the results, which is exactly what
pre-registration exists to prevent. Every future prereg states both branches before the
first call: (a) fails the bar and loses to a comparator, then the comparator runs; (b) fails
the bar but beats every comparator, then name in advance whether the model runs with a human
check, or nothing runs.

# AGENTS.md

Project: TypeSafe_Sandbox

## What this is
A sandbox for building against the TypeSafe System One API (the Jev model), which
returns typed judgments and probabilities instead of generated text. The API key is
NOT stored in this repo; see Secrets below for where it lives on each machine.
`setup_global_key.sh` installs the macOS side once per machine. `smoke_test.py` proves
the key resolves and the API answers.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

## Secrets

# Drive triage: pre-registration

Tenth item measured against the capability map. Registered 2026-09-26, **before any
model call**. The registering commit is the one that adds this file. Bars approved by
Eric on 2026-09-26. Consumer: the Flint project (`erash11/Flint`), which builds Eric's
sport-science knowledge base from his Drive.

**Governance: tier A.** The state is a Drive folder path, a file name, and up to 2,000
characters of a document's first page. The documents are coaching and research
material: books, papers, course handouts and slides. No athlete data. Flint's catalog
excludes DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports before anything
reaches this test.

## Question

Can Jev put the Drive files that Flint's keyword rules cannot place into the Zotero
taxonomy (14 domains, 96 topics, `zotero_classify/taxonomy.py`), confidently enough
that Flint can route them without a person reading each one?

## Gate check (capability map, three conditions)

1. **Genuinely fuzzy.** Deciding a coaching PDF's domain from its folder, name and
   first page is not a join, a threshold or a lookup.
2. **A consumer exists.** Flint routes every file by domain: into Zotero, the vault,
   the book queue or the transcription queue. It also builds a per-domain shortlist
   of files to ingest in full.
3. **Code baseline measured first.** Flint's keyword rules (`Flint/scripts/triage_rules.py`)
   classified 5,714 of 9,712 non-report files (59%). An md5 match against Zotero's
   Drive attachment store placed 81 more. The model pass covers only what code leaves.

## Sample (committed here: `drive_triage/sample.csv`)

200 files drawn by `Flint/scripts/draw_jev_sample.py`, seed 20260926, before any call.

- 100 from the 3,548 files the rules could not classify.
- 100 from the 5,254 files the rules did classify. These also measure the rules' own
  precision.
- Each half is stratified by source root, with proportional allocation.
- Excluded: Eric's own reports and dashboards, images, archives, and files already in
  Zotero.

## State per file

Folder path, file name, and the Zotero title where the md5 match recovered one. For
PDFs, Word files and slides, add up to 2,000 characters of first-page text. Video and
audio send path and name only. Files that are not synced locally (TB's Training Info)
are fetched with `gws` into a gitignored staging folder. State is built by code before
the answer key is written, and it is identical for every model.

## Questions

1. **Topic.** The `zotero_classify` topic Choice, unchanged (`classify.question()`),
   with the same domain fallback.
2. **Route.** One new Choice:
   - a research paper
   - a book or book chapter
   - course or lecture material
   - a coaching resource (programs, drills, templates, presentations)
   - Eric's own work
   - not sport-science material

## Answer key

Claude labels all 200 (domain, topic, route) from the same state, blind to every
model's answers, before the first Jev call. The labels are committed before Jev runs.

## Comparators (same 200, same state, same taxonomy)

- Flint's keyword rules, already run. On the unclassified half they count as misses.
- Haiku: one call per file, forced to name a topic.
- Codex: the same.

## Bars (fixed here; they never move)

| Measure | Bar |
|---|---|
| Jev confident: topic probability at or above the measured 0.50 cut | at least 60% of the 200 (120 files) |
| Jev domain accuracy on its confident answers, against the answer key | at least 90% |
| Jev versus Haiku: domain accuracy on Jev's confident subset | Jev at least equal to Haiku |
| Cost for the 200 | reported, no bar |

**Pass requires all three bars.** Topic-level and route accuracy are reported without
bars. The answer key comes before the models run, and the models do not define it.

## Answer-key audit (required step, capability map 2026-09-26)

Pull every file where Jev clears the 0.50 cut and its domain differs from the answer
key. Eric judges them blind: shuffled, sides hidden, input and the two answers only.
He sees at most 20 (a random 20 if there are more). The score on the original labels
decides pass or fail; the audited score is reported next to it.

## Outcomes

- **Pass.** Jev runs on Flint's remaining unclassified files. Below-cut answers fall
  back to domain, and anything still ambiguous goes to Claude.
- **Fail.** The best comparator does the pass. The result is written up here as the
  tenth entry on the map.
### 5. Tech Inventory athlete-data screening — the only candidate on the slate

- `Tech_Inventory_Analysis/scripts/aliases.py` `ATHLETE_DATA_CATEGORIES`; 188
  products, 75 current candidates, feeding the second-pass form (STATUS next #2).
  Rides the chartered deliverable (Kenny, 10-09; final run 09-29).
- Baseline: category membership flags every "performance" or "video" product and
  clears every comms/admin one.
- **Weakness:** state is a vendor name plus a unit. Without a one-line product
  description as state, Jev is guessing from a brand name. S.
- **Kill test:** hand-check 30 products; Jev must disagree with the category flag
  on ≥ 5 *and* be right on those, or the category rule stays.

### 6. Matchup injury/availability triage — timely, but the hard part is not Jev

- `MatchupAnalysis_FB2026/docs/weekly-routine.md`: the collection script "does not
  pull injury news and never will"; a Monday profile missed the opponent's injury
  report; Keys O1/O3 hinge on one player's status.
- Jev's part is a small Choice (out / doubtful / questionable / day-to-day /
  available / no info) over an article. **The real work is fetching the beat
  coverage**, which is code, and volume is a handful of players a week. M. Worth
  it only as part of a fetch step someone builds anyway.

## Demoted or held

- **`rerank_typesafe`** (map #1 since 09-20): the transcript sweep found **no
  evidence of misses** — all 14 memsearch mentions in 606 human messages over 42
  days are infrastructure failures. A pre-registered measurement is **in progress
  in another session** (`worktree-rerank-typesafe-measure`, commits `bfa5a79`,
  `340df41`); let that result decide. Not re-ranked here to avoid a conflict.
- **Connection-adjudicator pre-filter:** real signal (15 of 24 structural
  candidates rejected; ~13k tokens per 4 pairs), but Mac-only launchd and only two
  runs ever (08-02, 08-09). Confirm it still fires before anything else.
- **memlint dedup as a 3-level Score:** count the warnings and how many are real
  merges first.
- **Flush gate:** low volume (8 flushes in September). **Separately worth fixing:**
  ~282 "transcript missing" skips on the Windows `C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV`
  slug look like a path bug in the compiler.
- **BAIR proposal rubric:** textbook composite scoring, four proposals. Volume fails.
- **Coach-doc field-provenance check:** code records which field produced a
  number; Jev would only label claim type. Marginal.

## Near-misses worth recording so they are not re-proposed

- **Women's health survey (slate item):** IRB-approved study (IRB 2373733,
  Proulx). Data is not on disk, and third-party processing is governed by the IRB
  protocol, not Option C.
- **Point of attack from play text:** PFF already carries `rushing.run_position`;
  ESPN text only gives left/middle/right, which a regex reads.
- **Concussion RTP stage from notes:** 92 rows, median 3 words.
- **Kitman injury mechanism:** controlled vocabulary; the Risk engine lacks a field,
  not a judgment.
- **Email triage:** right shape, but morning-briefing was retired 08-14.
- **Tech Inventory survey free text:** hand-coded via 827 lines of `aliases.py` and
  finished for this cycle (1 prose row, 7 unmapped). Revisit next survey cycle.
- **Stop/PreToolUse guards:** "claimed done without verification" is a code check;
  a DexaProject guard would send the content it is guarding.

## Coverage — what was and was not seen

Seen: every folder under `~/Desktop/DEV` on Windows, the Windows Claude Code
transcripts (284 files, 606 human messages, last 42 days), the compiled knowledge
index and global memory. **Not seen:** Mac raw transcripts, the SecondBrain vault
(Mac-only), the fresh `pff.db` (Windows copy is from June 1), CFBD `playText` (not
on this box), Baylor Outlook. A Mac-side pass could add candidates; it is unlikely
to remove any above.

## Next actions

1. **Eric decides the Ath_Medicine governance question** (does Option C cover
   clinical note text?). Everything in #1 waits on it.
2. **Evidence Library kill test** (#2) needs no decision and no new data: run Jev
   over the 300 reviewed records with the rule's own fields. Tier A, pennies.
3. **Attendee-lookup baseline for Fireflies** (#4): pure code, settles whether a
   Jev build is needed.
4. Let the in-flight rerank measurement land before touching the map's #1.

Correction 2026-09-25: there was no Kitman vs Myelin decision, then or ever. The
vendor that came up is Myelin, a startup AMS Baylor is not pursuing; Kitman stays.

# Jev capability map

What TypeSafe's System One model (Jev) can and cannot do, and where it fits the work
we already run. Written 2026-09-19 after reading the full doc set. The vendor mirror in
`docs/vendor/typesafe/` is the reference; this file is the judgment.

## Jev in one screen

Jev is not a small LLM. It does not generate text at all. You send it a **state** (a
string, JSON object, or array) and a map of typed **questions**, and it returns typed
answers with calibrated probabilities. Three question types, and that is the entire
surface:

| Type | Answers | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `Noul` | Is this statement true? | `noul`, a probability from 0 to 1. No separate confidence. |
| `Choice` | Which of these options? | `choice`, `probabilities` over every option, `confidence` |
| `Score` | Which level on this rubric? | `score` (can land between levels), `legend`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |

Four properties matter more than the API shape:

1. **Every question in a request is evaluated independently and in parallel.** One
   answer never becomes hidden context for another. Adding questions barely changes
   latency and costs only the question's own tokens. Batching 13 questions over a
   54k-character document instead of sending 13 calls was 12.2x cheaper and 10.0x
   faster with *identical* answers.
2. **Answers are constrained to the options you supply.** The model cannot return a
   value outside your set, so code never parses prose. This is why "select, do not
   generate" is the core move: find candidates in code, let Jev pick one.
3. **Confidence is a second decision axis.** The answer says what; confidence says
   whether to act. Low confidence is a usable signal, not a failure.
4. **Judgments become reusable data.** Score once, then re-weight, re-threshold, and
   re-rank in code forever with no further calls.

The design rule the docs repeat hardest: **decompose**. Never ask one broad question.
Ask each independent factor separately and combine the answers with weights you own in
code. When priorities change you edit a coefficient, not a prompt.

## Limits and failure modes

Hard limits (`jev-1.13`, verified on the Models page):

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Price | $0.042 per million input tokens. Output tokens free. |
| Context | 64k per request; 32k for `state` plus the longest question |
| Choice options | 255 maximum, roughly 240 before reliability drops |
| Score levels | 2 minimum, 10 maximum. An 11th returns a server error. |
| Input | Text only. String, JSON object, or array. No image, audio, video. |
| Rate | 250,000 tokens/sec, 1,200 requests/min, adjusted without notice |
| Latency | About 100 to 115 ms per call, measured across two cookbooks |
| Language | English is best. Other languages accepted, lower accuracy. |

Documented failure modes, from the jev-1.13 jaggedness page:

1. **Not a calculator.** Counting, arithmetic, and comparing numeric representations
   are all unreliable. Keep math in code.
2. **Dates are read as text, not ordered quantities.** It cannot reliably tell which
   date is earlier or whether one falls in a window. Extract the parts as Choices over
   enumerated options, assemble and compare in code.
3. **Literal reading.** It answers the question you wrote, not the one you meant. If
   you find yourself explaining what you really meant, that explanation is the missing
   half of the instruction.
4. **Context rot.** Accuracy falls as the state grows with irrelevant content. Filter
   in code first, send only what the question needs.
5. **Not adversarial by default.** State is data, and injected instructions can move
   the answer. Never a security boundary on its own.
6. **No structural invariants.** A Noul and an equivalent yes/no Choice are different
   questions and give different numbers. P(A) and 1 - P(not A) do not have to agree;
   one measured pair summed to 1.19. Never carry a threshold tuned on one primitive
   over to another.
7. **Consistent but not deterministic.** Mean run-to-run probability standard deviation
   is 0.0102, far tighter than any LLM tested, but labels near a threshold still flip:
   2 of 8 questions changed their top label across 15 repeats. The fix is an explicit
   uncertain band (Noul 0.30 to 0.70, Choice top probability under 0.60) routed to a
   person, which took label agreement to 99.2% while still auto-deciding 74.2%.

## Where it fits what we run

Governance tier controls everything, because Jev is a cloud API and Baylor data rules
apply. **A** = no athlete or health data leaves the machine. **B** = possible only
after de-identification. **C** = blocked without IT approval.

| Cookbook / pattern | Our workflow | Primitive sketch | Tier | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `skill_suggestion` | Pick 1 skill from ~155 for each prompt | Choice over all skills + 3 Noul gates, then rerank top 3 | A | S |
| `classification_using_confidence` | Tag Zotero papers by topic; report a broader topic when unsure instead of dropping | 1 Choice over the taxonomy, back off one level below 0.9 confidence | A | S |
| `rerank_typesafe` | memsearch result quality | 1 Noul per query-candidate pair, sort by noul | A | S |
| `classifying_rag_passages` | Filter what reaches a prompt from memsearch or the vault | 4 Nouls: relevant, has evidence, contradicts premise, injection | A | M |
| `entity_alignment` | Athlete ID reconciliation across Catapult, VALD, Perch, S2, roster | 1 Score with 3 levels (different / curator / same) + 1 Noul per field | B | M |
| `composite-scoring` | Project registry ranking, prioritization slate | 1 Score per dimension, weights in code | A | S |
| `semantic_find` | Query the NCAA charter, policies, contracts by plain question | Choice over tagged line IDs + Noul "does an answer exist" | A | S |
| `citation_check` | Verify the Research in 5 deck and status report before sending | String-match the quote in code, then 1 Choice: supports / contradicts / says nothing | A | M |
| `sde_cascade` | Verify Claude's own extractions before they land in STATUS.md or the vault | 1 Noul per field framed so true means escalate, gate on max | A | M |
| `autoresearch_feature_discovery` | Turn free-text notes into numeric model features | Score + Noul per feature, answers become CatBoost columns | B/C | L |
| `function_calling` | Natural language to our own CLIs (`portfolio.py`, report commands) | 1 Choice over commands + 1 Choice per closed-set argument + a `stated` Noul | A | M |
| `hierarchical_classification` | Deep taxonomy walks (CPC-style research trees) | 1 Choice per level, beam search over probabilities | A | L |
| `llm_guardrails` | Screen anything scraped or pasted before an agent acts on it | Noul battery + severity Score, thresholds per policy | A | M |
| `autoresearch_feature_discovery` | PP_Recruiting pre-portal screening | 20 to 30 narrow Nouls and Scores per scouting note, answers join the percentile matrix as columns | A, see note | L |

### PP_Recruiting: not now, and what would change that

Assessed 2026-09-19 against the 009 workbook and the 09-16 validation run. **Nothing
here is worth building today.** Recording it so it does not get re-litigated.

The screening engine itself is out of scope permanently: it compares percentiles to
thresholds (75th percentile, 0.375 elite share, Impact 90+), which is the exact thing
the jaggedness page says Jev is unreliable at. Its real weakness is calibration, not
judgment quality. The 09-16 validation ran low by 0.77 tiers on average, 1.25 against
Power Four, and caught 5 of 15 defensive players. That is fixed by more graded
validation players and code, not by a different model.

Two candidates that looked like fits and are not:

- **Player entity resolution.** Collapses to a code join. Telemetry carries a stable
  `PlayerId`, and `load_leaderboard.py` already joins Player Traits to Advanced Stats
  on it. The one open cross-source question (Jordan Church) is a single name against
  the recap list, and 30 of 30 transfers already matched by hand. One player is not a
  pattern.
- **Role assignment (WR/SLOT, END/JACK, CB/STAR).** The live blocker on deliverable
  010, so this was the one worth wanting. Inputs are alignment codes (OWR/SWR, ILB/OLB,
  OCB/SCB), already deterministic in both scripts, plus percentiles. Nothing
  text-shaped to decide on.

**The one real fit is text to features, and it has no input corpus.** It aims straight
at the weakest spot, defense, where percentile data is thinnest and film language is
richest. But pre-portal FCS and G6 players at week 5 to 6 have Telemetry percentiles
and nothing else. **Trigger: revisit when scouting text exists** — either the personnel
staff member starts writing evals on REVIEW rows (the 30 to 50 names per position he
asked for), or players hit the portal and recruiting services publish on them. Shape
when that day comes: not "is this a good corner," but 20 to 30 independent narrow
questions per note (*Noul: the note describes him redirecting without losing speed.
Noul: the note describes him losing leverage against bigger blockers. Score 1 to 5: how
much of this note is about his hands.*) in one request, weights in our code.

Two constraints that narrow it further whenever it is revisited:

- **Jev cannot live in the workbook.** The staff member runs the weekly refresh himself
  in Excel and Power Query. Any Jev step is Eric-run preprocessing, so it must be
  batch-once like the baseline load, or a standing Monday job. That rules out most of
  what is otherwise tempting, and the weekly refresh is the one piece someone else runs
  without Eric — a network call on that path is a straight downgrade.
- **Tier A here is about the wrong risk.** These are public college players, not Baylor
  athletes, so the health-data tiers do not bind. But Telemetry grades are licensed
  vendor data, and sending 8,761 rows to `api.typesafe.ai` is a question under
  **Telemetry's own terms on third-party processing**. Settle that before any of this,
  including anything small.

## What this unlocks that we cannot do today

Four of these are genuinely new capability, not a cheaper version of something we have.

**1. Free text becomes model features.** The autoresearch cookbook turns 2,000 wine
tasting notes into 67 numeric columns and trains CatBoost on them. Held-out RMSE went
from 3.09 (predict the mean) to 2.47 (word counts) to 2.15 (just ask Jev for the score)
to **1.77** (38 decomposed feature questions). The decomposition beat asking directly,
which is the whole thesis. Our equivalent: coach notes, wellness comments, RTP
narrative, and scouting text become inputs to a model instead of prose nobody scores.
Start on CFB scouting or public text, which is tier A. Athlete narrative is tier B or C
and waits.

**2. ~~Athlete ID reconciliation without a threshold to fit.~~ WITHDRAWN 2026-09-20 —
measured, and there is no problem here to solve.** ~~We have the same name spelled four
ways across Catapult, VALD, Perch, S2, and the roster, and today that is
hand-matching.~~ The entity-alignment recipe makes the three Score levels *be* the three
actions (leave unlinked, send to a curator, merge), so there is no number to tune, and
rides three Nouls along in the same request to tell the curator which field disagrees.
On 450 pairs it settled 89% automatically and queued 11%. Athlete names are PII, so
this is tier B and needs a de-identified key mapping first.

> **What the measurement found** (`athlete_matching/measure_residue.py`, full write-up
> in `ATHLETE_KEY_MAPPING.md`):
>
> - The premise above is **false**. The name is not "spelled four ways": of the 300
>   athletes that found any counterpart above 80, **287 settle on exact normalised
>   string equality**, every one scoring 100, with nothing in the 95–99 band. The
>   residue is **13 pairs**. (Settled means string-equal, not confirmed same person —
>   see the doc's caveats; with no DOB that gap is a missing attribute, not a
>   judgment a model could supply.)
> - The 89%/11% figure quoted here is from the cookbook's own dataset, not ours.
>   Measured on Baylor's data the split is 96%/4%, and the 96% needs no model —
>   `lower()`, strip punctuation, drop suffixes, collapse initials, join.
> - The tier-B blocker is also moot twice over: Eric cleared Option C on 2026-09-20,
>   and there is nothing left worth sending anyway.
>
> This entry stays visible rather than being deleted, because the reasoning that put
> it at #2 was sound and only an actual measurement moved it. The lesson worth keeping
> is that it was ranked on an assumed data condition nobody had checked — the same way
> the PP_Recruiting entity-resolution case was proposed before a `grep` killed it.

**3. Ask a policy document a plain question.** Tag each line with an ID, send one
Choice over the line IDs plus one Noul asking whether the document answers at all. The
Noul is what stops it from confidently pointing at the closest wrong line: on a
question the GitHub ToS does not answer, the top line still scored 0.86 while `exists`
read 0.14. Point it at the NCAA charter and Baylor policy. Cap is 255 lines per request; longer documents need a two-stage narrowing.

**4. A cheap verifier in front of expensive output.** This is the one I would not have
predicted. Every deliverable that leaves this machine (status report, Research in 5
deck, evidence brief) can be screened per-claim before it goes out, at roughly $0.00005
a call. The sde_cascade rules for a good verifier signal: one narrow grounded yes/no
per field, framed so *true* means escalate, aggregated with `max` so one confident red
flag survives instead of being averaged into silence.

## Where not to use it

- **Numeric verification on its own.** Correcting my 09-19 chat answer: the citation
  pipeline does apply to the TOS brief, but the part that catches a misquoted number is
  the **code string-match in step 1**, not Jev. Jev's Choice catches "this section says
  the opposite of the claim" (it flagged one at 0.99 confidence). Use both, and do not
  ask Jev whether 3.2 equals 3.2.
- **Date and window arithmetic.** Kickoff-time math in the sleep scheduler, GPS pull
  windows, availability windows. Extract parts, compute in code.
- **Anything that needs prose out.** It does not generate. Output is free because there
  is none.
- **Any per-athlete GPS, force plate, DEXA, or S2 record**, until Baylor IT says
  otherwise. Our own smoke test already posted a hamstring-tightness note to
  `api.typesafe.ai`. It was synthetic, and it shows how small the slip is.
- **As a security boundary.** The injection Noul is a filter, not a gate. Treat every
  passage that reaches a prompt as untrusted regardless of its score.

## Sequence

**First: the skill router.** It pays off across all 23 projects rather than one, and the
fit question I flagged on 09-19 is now resolved: 182 skills render to 16,089 characters,
about 4k tokens, so our ~155 fit inside the 32k budget with room to spare. Measured on
488 requests against Haiku 4.5, wrong skill loads fell 16.8% to 7.3% and needless loads
9.8% to 4.0%. It fixed 37 requests and broke 7.

Design constraints that are not optional here:

- It runs as a `UserPromptSubmit` hook, which means a network call on **every** prompt.
  Our memsearch hook is currently failing with `ETIMEDOUT` 8x consecutively. Same
  fragility class.
- Therefore: hard timeout around 2 seconds, **fail open** (no suggestion, never a
  blocked prompt), and no retries in the hot path.
- Use the cookbook's exact wording, including "Ignore this if it does not fit what the
  user actually asked for." Pushing harder wins compliance on wrong suggestions too.
- Patch both `.claude/hooks/` and `.codex/hooks/`, and run it under the shell the
  MSYS-stall fix settled on, not Git Bash.

**Next two, in order:** Zotero backlog classification with confidence backoff (tier A,
small, and the 1,018-papers-for-$0.08 demo is literally the same job), then the
deliverable verifier on the status report and Research in 5.

## Re-ranked 2026-09-20, after five items were resolved

All three of the original sequence shipped. Five of fourteen rows are now closed:
`skill_suggestion` (live), `classification_using_confidence` (1,418 records),
`citation_check` (live and gating, 6 of 6 after the apparatus strip),
`entity_alignment` (**withdrawn**, measured) and PP_Recruiting screening (**rejected**).

### The rule this project earned, stated as a gate rather than a story

Every item that was measured moved, and every one moved *down*. Entity alignment was
ranked second and was withdrawn. PP_Recruiting offered two obvious fits that both
collapsed into code. The Zotero renames were recommended skip. `AUTO_ACCEPT` came in
at the cookbook's 0.90 and measured to 0.80; the Zotero cutoff came in at 0.90 and
measured to 0.50. That is not bad luck, it is a missing gate. **Build only where all
three hold:**

1. **The answer is genuinely fuzzy** — not a join, not a threshold, not a lookup.
2. **Something already consumes the answer.** No consumer, no build. This is the
   Zotero-renames test.
3. **A code baseline was measured first.** If deterministic code gets most of the way,
   the model is decoration.

Each withdrawn item failed a *different* one of these, which is why no single check
would have caught them. Entity alignment failed (1) — exact string equality settled
287 of 300 and fuzzy matching contributed zero settled pairs. The Zotero renames
failed (2). The prose-number work nearly failed (3) and was saved only because the
band was measured before and after.

### Answer-key audit: a required step in every pre-registered test (added 2026-09-26)

Three measurements found a bad answer key, not a bad model: the surgery count (17 by
regex, 22 under blind labels), the Evidence Library tags (the reviewed labels sided
with Jev on 5 of 8 rules-picks), and the spring notes (role words the labels missed).
The "Just Ask Jev" paper (arXiv 2609.29429) reports the same on three public
benchmarks. So every pre-registration now carries this step, written down before the
first call:

1. **Pull the confident disagreements.** Every item where Jev's probability clears the
   pre-registered confidence cut and its answer differs from the label. Fix the cut
   in the pre-registration, not after seeing results.
2. **Eric judges them blind.** Shuffle, hide which side said what, show only the input
   and the two answers. He marks label right, Jev right, or unclear.
3. **Report both scores.** The pre-registered score on the original labels decides
   pass or fail, and the bar never moves. The audited score is reported next to it,
   and the count of labels changed is a finding in its own right.
4. **Cap the audit.** At most 20 items. If there are more than 20 confident
   disagreements, audit a random 20 and report the rate. More than that is a label
   problem worth its own write-up.

What this is not: a way to rescue a failed test. A test that fails on the original
labels and passes on the audited ones is reported as FAIL, with the audit as the reason
to re-run against fresh labels.

### Next three

> **ANSWERED 2026-09-20 — `sde_cascade` is a CODE LINTER, not a Jev build.** The
> inventory below was run: 10 handoffs per sample, **7.7% Jev-shaped** against the
> pre-registered 25% threshold, **7.7–10.8% across four seeds**, and 88.4% of
> checkable claims settled by `stat`, `git`, a file test or a re-run. Full write-up
> in `docs/SDE_CASCADE_SCOPING.md`; code in `sde_cascade/inventory.py`.
>
> **Stated precisely, because the margin is narrower than the headline:** the
> decision holds on the measured share and under either adversarial bound alone, on
> every seed. Stacking *both* bounds at once — assume every ambiguous statement is
> Jev-shaped AND strip the third of the code bucket whose only evidence is a
> non-path quoted token — gives 21.6–29.9%, which crosses 25% on 2 of 4 seeds. Code
> linter is the right call; "not a close call" is not.
>
> The best single check is *does every backticked path still resolve?*, and it
> covers **39.3%** of code claims — not the 84.9% the shape table suggests, which
> counts any quoted token. The prototype's real cost is false alarms, not coverage:
> the unresolved rate walked from 43% to 24% **without finding one extra file**,
> purely by learning that `~/DEV/` is the Mac layout, that cross-repo references are
> the common case, and that the SecondBrain vault is Mac-only. Fourth item
> measurement has moved down the map.

**1. `sde_cascade` — but scoped, and the scoping is the deliverable.**
The target surface is real and large: **126 `STATUS.md` files and 79 handoffs** in
`~/DEV`. The failure is live — on 2026-09-20 three documents asserted the running
header was stripped when it removed nothing, and this very file's sibling asserted
the citation band "is the bibliography", which aimed the session's top-priority task
one layer too shallow.

But "verify our state claims" is a category, not a build, and as a category it has
exactly the smell that got entity alignment withdrawn. Sort the claims first:

| claim shape | example from 09-20 | who checks it |
|---|---|---|
| a date, count, path, or "does X exist" | "`perch.duckdb` last written 2026-04-30" | **code** — `stat`, `git`, a byte count |
| a step's effect | "the running header is stripped" | **code** — assert `chars_removed > 0` |
| prose about what a linked document says | "PRs #7 and #8 are not merged"; "`run_pipeline.py` exists" | **Jev** — this is `citation_check`'s exact shape |
| a causal claim | "the band *is* the bibliography" | **neither** — needs a controlled measurement |

So the honest first step is not code, it is an **inventory**: take ten handoffs,
classify every claim into those four rows, and count. If the Jev-shaped row is under
about a quarter, `sde_cascade` is a code linter that needs no model, and should be
built as one. Same pattern as `measure_residue.py` — measure the residue, let the
number decide. **Do that inventory before writing any Jev call.**

> **ANSWERED 2026-09-21: `rerank_typesafe` is NOT built.** Ten real recall
> questions, pre-registered rule: hit@5 4 of 10 (5 audited), but only 1 to 2 misses
> sit in ranks 6 to 20, against the 3 needed. The misses are context-free questions,
> an unindexed folder and vendor-doc dilution, none of which a reranker can fix. Fifth
> item measured off the map. Write-up: `docs/RERANK_MEASUREMENT.md`.

**2. `rerank_typesafe` — second because it is the one that can be measured cheaply.**
memsearch is rung L1 of the retrieval ladder in `memory-write`, hit on every "did we
already…?", against a haystack of 126 STATUS files, 79 handoffs, ~230 compiled
articles and the daily logs. One Noul per query-candidate pair, tier A, small.

Pre-register the test before building: pull **ten real past questions** from the
transcripts, record whether the right answer is in the current top-5, and only build
if it is not. If the hit rate is already 9 of 10, reranking buys nothing and this is
the Zotero-renames trap wearing a different hat.

**3. `composite-scoring` — possible, with the caveat stated up front.**
The consumer is real (`project-triage/slate.py`, with tests; the slate is capped at 5
and full). But the obvious test — does Jev's ordering match Eric's? — **proves
nothing on five items**, where chance agreement is high, and the slate is Eric's
call by design rather than a bottleneck. Either find a bigger ranking surface (the
full project registry, not the slate) or accept it as low-value and skip it. Do not
run the five-item comparison and treat agreement as validation.

### Blocked on access, not on effort — and both share one unblock

- **`semantic_find`**: no longer has a target. It was aimed at Kitman and Myelin vendor
  documents. There is no AMS decision for it to feed: Myelin is a startup AMS Baylor
  is not pursuing, and Kitman stays (corrected 2026-09-25).
- **`autoresearch_feature_discovery`**: the biggest genuine upside on this map
  (decomposition beat asking directly, RMSE 1.77 against 2.15) and governance is no
  longer the gate — but **there is no input corpus on this box.** Checked the Kitman
  injury export: 29 columns, and the only long fields are `Pathology`, which is a
  controlled clinical vocabulary rather than prose, and `Game Opposition`, which is
  team names. No narrative column at all. That is the PP_Recruiting finding repeating.

Both need access to a system that holds the prose — Kitman's narrative fields behind a
key that is not read-only, or Baylor Outlook. **One access conversation unblocks two
items**, which makes it worth more than either alone.

### Demoted on inspection

**`function_calling`** reads better on the map than it is. Claude Code already *is*
the natural-language-to-CLI layer, so routing a chat request through Jev adds a step
where a working one exists. The one place it is not redundant is the same place the
skill router paid off: **as a hook**, deciding without a conversation turn. Build it
only in that form, or not at all.

## Drive triage, the tenth measurement (scored 2026-09-28): FAIL, used anyway

Pre-registration: `docs/DRIVE_TRIAGE_PREREG.md`. Results: `drive_triage/results.md`.

| Bar | Needed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Confident (p >= 0.50) | 60% of 200 | 166/200 (83%): pass |
| Domain accuracy, confident answers | 90% | 127/166 (76.5%): **fail** |
| Jev vs Haiku, same subset | Jev >= Haiku | 127 vs 108: pass |

- **Jev won every comparison and still missed the absolute bar.** On all 200 it beat Haiku on
  domain (74.5% vs 66.0%) and topic (63.5% vs 52.0%). Codex (200/200) tied it on domain
  (148 vs 149) but was worse on the unclassified half (75 vs 81) and has no confidence signal.
- **Where it held up:** the files the keyword rules could not place, which is the population
  Flint actually needs. There Jev's confident answers were right on 85.2% (69/81). On files the
  rules had already placed, it was right on only 68.2%.
- **What hurt:** the state. 87 of 200 files had no first-page text (video, scans, empty Drive
  entries). A file name and a folder cannot carry a 90% bar.
- **Decision (Eric, 2026-09-28):** Jev does Flint's pass, with Eric's shortlist approval kept
  as the check. The verdict stays FAIL, and this is not a rescue under the audit rule.

**The lesson for the next pre-registration.** The fail branch said "the best comparator does
the pass". It never said what happens when the model fails its bar but beats every
comparator. That left a decision to be made after the results, which is exactly what
pre-registration exists to prevent. Every future prereg states both branches before the
first call: (a) fails the bar and loses to a comparator, then the comparator runs; (b) fails
the bar but beats every comparator, then name in advance whether the model runs with a human
check, or nothing runs.

## Re-ranked 2026-09-21, after a sweep of every project

Full ranking, kill tests and coverage: `docs/handoffs/2026-09-21-leverage-sweep-all-projects.md`.

- **Text-to-features is no longer blocked on a corpus.** `Ath_Medicine` holds 7,555
  medical diagnostics notes (3,924 cleaned) already read by six regex/TF-IDF scripts feeding
  the annual report and the 534-athlete rollup; `Football/SpringPlayerEvals_SymAnalysis`
  holds 99 x 4 department notes behind the Coach One-Pager. The closeout's "one access
  conversation unblocks two items" now holds for neither (`semantic_find` had no real
  target; see the 2026-09-25 correction above).
- **New order:** (1) Ath_Medicine notes, surgery tagger first, gated on Eric extending
  Option C to clinical note text; (2) Evidence Library domain tags, the only item with a
  ready labelled set (300 reviewed; regex exact-set 55/300; only 151/707 overlap the
  Zotero labels, so not a reuse); (3) spring exit notes, judged against the Claude pass
  (rho 0.30, n 34), never by fitting weights; (4) Fireflies meeting to project, only if
  an attendee lookup settles under 80%; (5) Tech Inventory athlete-data screening, the
  one item on the slate; (6) matchup injury triage, where the fetch is the real work.
- **`rerank_typesafe`:** no transcript evidence of misses (14 memsearch mentions, all
  infrastructure). Its pre-registered measurement is running in another worktree; that
  result decides its rank, not this sweep.

## Corrections to the 2026-09-19 chat answer

Four things the full read changed:

1. The 32k fit question is answered: 155 skills fit comfortably.
2. Citation checking is **not** ruled out for the TOS brief. See above.
3. Fireflies renaming is workable as *selection*: code or an LLM proposes 3 to 5
   candidate titles, Jev picks one. It still cannot write a title, and it is still
   gated on stripping athlete names from the summary.
4. Memory deduplication is the entity-alignment shape (a 3-level Score whose levels are
   the actions), not a Noul with a threshold.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Minimal bounded client for the TypeSafe System One endpoint. Stdlib only.

Lifted from the skill router's `ask()`, which is the only HTTP path in this repo that
has been reviewed. The important property is the same here even though a batch job is
not latency-critical: **the timeout is real wall-clock time, not a socket timeout.**

`urlopen(timeout=)` bounds each individual blocking operation, so DNS, connect, TLS
and every body read each get the full value; a server trickling bytes never trips it.
The request therefore runs on a daemon thread and is abandoned if it overruns. In a
batch of 1,400 that is the difference between one slow record and a job that never
finishes.

NOTE: `skill_router/router.py` on branch `worktree-jev-skill-router` still carries its
own copy of this logic. When that branch merges, point it at this module so there is
one HTTP path rather than two that can drift.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
import threading
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

ENDPOINT = os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT", "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone")
MODEL = os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_MODEL", "jev-latest")
MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024


class JevError(RuntimeError):
    """Anything that stopped us getting a usable answer."""


def api_key() -> str:
    """Env var first, then ~/.claude/typesafe.env.

    The key must keep its `apikey_` prefix. A 401 means the key value is wrong; a 422
    means the request body is. That split is the fastest way to tell which end is at
    fault, and it has cost this project time before.
    """
    key = os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_API_KEY")
    if key and key.strip():
        return key.strip()
    env_file = Path(os.path.expanduser("~")) / ".claude" / "typesafe.env"
    try:
        for line in env_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
            name, _, value = line.strip().partition("=")
            if name.strip() == "TYPESAFE_API_KEY" and value.strip():
                return value.strip().strip("\"'")
    except OSError:
        pass
    raise JevError(
        "no TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the environment or ~/.claude/typesafe.env"
    )


def system_one(state, questions: dict, key: str, timeout: float = 20.0) -> dict:
    """POST one request and return its `answers` map. Raises JevError on anything else.

    No retries here on purpose: the caller owns retry policy, because what is safe to
    retry in a resumable batch job is not what is safe in a hook.
    """
    body = json.dumps(
        {"state": state, "model": MODEL, "questions": questions}
    ).encode("utf-8")
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        ENDPOINT,
        data=body,
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {key}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        method="POST",
    )

    outcome: dict = {}

    def perform() -> None:
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=timeout) as response:
                raw = response.read(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES)
            outcome["data"] = json.loads(raw.decode("utf-8"))
        except BaseException as error:  # noqa: BLE001 - handed back to the caller
            outcome["error"] = error

    worker = threading.Thread(target=perform, daemon=True)
    worker.start()
    worker.join(timeout)
    if worker.is_alive():
        raise JevError(f"wall-clock timeout after {timeout}s")
    if "error" in outcome:
        raise JevError(f"{type(outcome['error']).__name__}: {outcome['error']}")

    payload = outcome.get("data")
    if not isinstance(payload, dict):
        raise JevError("response is not an object")
    answers = payload.get("answers")
    if not isinstance(answers, dict) or not answers:
        raise JevError("response carried no answers")
    return answers
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run Jev on the 200 pre-registered Drive triage files (DRIVE_TRIAGE_PREREG.md).

    python drive_triage/run_jev.py            # resumable; finished rows are skipped

One request per file, two questions: the zotero_classify topic Choice, unchanged
(`classify.question()`), and the pre-registered route Choice. State comes from
drive_triage/private/state.jsonl (built by build_state.py, sha256 committed with the
answer key). Every raw answer is appended to drive_triage/runs/jev.jsonl before any
threshold is applied. The file holds sample ids and answers only, no document text.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import sys
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE.parent / "zotero_classify"))
import classify  # noqa: E402
import jev_client  # noqa: E402
import taxonomy  # noqa: E402

ROUTES = {
    "a research paper": "A journal article, review, thesis or research report.",
    "a book or book chapter": "A published book, textbook, manual of book length, or a chapter from one.",
    "course or lecture material": "Slides, notes or recordings from a course, certification, seminar or conference lecture.",
    "a coaching resource (programs, drills, templates, presentations)":
        "Practical coaching material: training programs, drills, templates, handouts, coach presentations.",
    "Eric's own work": "Material Eric Rash wrote or built himself: his reports, programs, plans, presentations or courses.",
    "not sport-science material": "Admin, personal, receipts, travel, system files, raw data or anything outside sport science.",
}


def questions() -> dict:
    q = classify.question()
    q["route"] = {
        "type": "choice",
        "instructions": "What kind of file is this, as its folder, name and first page describe it?",
        "criteria": dict(ROUTES),
    }
    return q


def run_one(row: dict, key: str) -> dict:
    started = time.monotonic()
    answers = jev_client.system_one(row["state"], questions(), key, timeout=30.0)
    topic, route = answers.get("topic"), answers.get("route")
    if not isinstance(topic, dict) or topic.get("choice") not in taxonomy.DOMAIN_OF:
        raise jev_client.JevError(f"bad topic answer: {topic!r}")
    if not isinstance(route, dict) or route.get("choice") not in ROUTES:
        raise jev_client.JevError(f"bad route answer: {route!r}")
    top = sorted((topic.get("probabilities") or {}).items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:5]
    return {
        "sample_id": row["sample_id"],
        "topic": topic["choice"],
        "domain": taxonomy.domain_of(topic["choice"]),
        "confidence": round(float(topic["confidence"]), 4),
        "top": [[n, round(float(p), 4)] for n, p in top],
        "route": route["choice"],
        "route_confidence": round(float(route.get("confidence") or 0), 4),
        "ms": int((time.monotonic() - started) * 1000),
    }


def main() -> int:
    state = [json.loads(l) for l in (HERE / "private" / "state.jsonl").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines() if l.strip()]
    out = HERE / "runs" / "jev.jsonl"
    out.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    done = set()
    if out.exists():
        for line in out.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
            try:
                done.add(json.loads(line)["sample_id"])
            except (ValueError, KeyError):
                continue
    todo = [r for r in state if r["sample_id"] not in done]
    print(f"{len(state)} files, {len(done)} done, {len(todo)} to do")
    key = jev_client.api_key()
    failures = []
    with out.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as fh, ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
        def work(row):
            try:
                return row, run_one(row, key), None
            except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
                return row, None, f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"
        for row, res, err in pool.map(work, todo):
            if err:
                failures.append((row["sample_id"], err))
                continue
            fh.write(json.dumps(res, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    print(f"failures: {len(failures)}")
    for f in failures[:10]:
        print(" ", *f)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
# Drive triage: the Jev pilot (run record)

Pre-registration: `docs/DRIVE_TRIAGE_PREREG.md` (bars fixed 2026-09-26, before any call).
Sample: `sample.csv` (200 files, seed 20260926).

## Order of work (each step committed before the next)

1. `build_state.py`: state for all 200, built by code. Written to `private/state.jsonl`
   (gitignored: first-page text of Drive documents).
   **state.jsonl sha256 `779d3ff481960373070214bda7bdfa4079abd68fed20a7f57a3956c99c06aada`**
2. `answer_key.csv`: Claude's labels (topic, derived domain, route) for all 200. They were written by one
   fresh agent that read only `private/state.jsonl` and `taxonomy_for_key.md`. It saw no Flint
   label, no `sample.csv` column beyond what the state carries, and no model answer.
   It was committed and pushed before the first Jev call.
3. `run_jev.py`: Jev, one request per file (topic Choice unchanged from `classify.question()`
   plus the route Choice defined in the script). Raw answers in `runs/jev.jsonl`.
4. Comparators (Haiku, Codex) and scoring against the bars.

## State as built (2026-09-28)

| Extraction | Files |
|---|---:|
| First page (median about 1,870 characters) | 113 |
| Path and name only (video, audio, data files; by design) | 53 |
| PDF with no text layer (scans) | 18 |
| Empty in Drive (size 0; the Drive entry holds no content) | 7 |
| Not a readable PDF (3 macOS `._` resource forks, 1 damaged file) | 4 |
| Legacy Office format (.doc, .ppt) | 3 |
| Encrypted PDF | 1 |
| PDF parser limit | 1 |

So 87 of 200 files carry no first-page text. That is thinner than the pre-registration
assumed, but identical for every model and for the answer key.

Method notes:
- All documents were fetched by Drive id with `gws`, one method for every root.
- There is no Anthropic API key on this machine. Haiku runs through headless
  `claude -p --model claude-haiku-4-5`, one call per file with the same state and the same
  forced topic.

## Result (2026-09-28)

Scored with `score.py`; the full table is in `results.md`. Verdict on the original labels:
**FAIL** (confident 83%: pass; domain accuracy on confident answers 76.5% against a 90% bar:
fail; Jev 127 vs Haiku 108 on the same subset: pass). Eric chose Jev for Flint's pass anyway,
with his shortlist approval kept as the check (`docs/JEV_CAPABILITY_MAP.md`, tenth measurement).

- Haiku: 200/200, 0 parse failures, about 35-60 s per call via headless `claude -p`.
- Codex: 200/200, 0 failures, about 70 s per call; finished in foreground chunks after the
  low-memory reaper stopped two background runs. it tied Jev on domain over all 200 (148 vs 149) and edged it on Jev's confident subset (131 vs 127), topic (66.0% vs 63.5%) and route (72.0% vs 66.5%). But on the unclassified half, Flint's target, it was worse (75 vs 81 of 100; 65 vs 69 on Jev's confident 81). It has no confidence signal and takes about 70 s per file against Jev's 0.3 s, so Jev stays the choice.
- Cost: `run_jev.py` records latency only (56.4 s total over 200 calls), not credits, so the
  cost line the prereg asks for is latency plus call count.
- Audit: `private/audit_sheet.md` (20 of 39 confident disagreements) is waiting on Eric.

content.content:
# Noul

> A Noul question asks the model to evaluate a yes/no question and return the probability that the answer is yes.


Use a Noul when the answer is yes or no. For example, does this message ask for a refund, does this resume mention distributed systems, does this comment contain personal data. If the answer is one of several options, use a [Choice](/primitives/choice). If it's a position on a spectrum, use a [Score](/primitives/score). [Choose a question type](/primitives#choose-a-question-type) compares all three.

A Noul answer is a single number, `noul`, the probability that the answer is yes.

## Writing a Noul question

A Noul question evaluates a single yes/no question (or statement). It is defined by its `instructions`: the yes/no question to evaluate. It's good practice to phrase it so a high probability means "yes", so that the returned answer is unambiguous in its meaning.

You can optionally add `criteria` with `true` and `false` descriptions to clarify what each outcome means, which can be helpful when the question itself has more nuance to explain. Try your Noul question prompts with and without criteria to see which works better in your use-case.

## Request

| Field          | Required | Description                                                                  |
| -------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `type`         | Yes      | Must be `"noul"`.                                                            |
| `instructions` | Yes      | The yes/no question or statement to evaluate.                                |
| `criteria`     | No       | Optional `{ true, false }` descriptions clarifying what a yes and a no mean. |

<TypesafeExample
  display="request"
  example={{
state: 'I have asked three times now. Can I please just talk to a real person?',
selectedModels: ['jev-latest'],
questions: {
  is_human_escalation: {
    type: 'noul',
    instructions: 'Is the customer asking for a human agent?',
  },
  is_repeat_contact: {
    type: 'noul',
    instructions: 'Has the customer contacted support about this before?',
    criteria: {
      true: 'Mentions a prior attempt, ticket, or that they have asked before',
      false: 'No sign of any previous contact',
    },
  },
},
}}
/>

## Response

```json theme={null}
{
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "answers": {
    "is_human_escalation": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.99
    },
    "is_repeat_contact": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.93
    }
  },
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 360,
    "output_tokens": 39
  }
}
```

`noul` ranges from 0 to 1, representing the probability that the answer is **yes**. Most often you will threshold it into a boolean when your code needs a hard decision.

## Noul does not return a separate confidence value

A value near 1 means a strong yes. A value near 0 means a strong no. A value near 0.5 gives yes and no similar probability.

For "Is the candidate strong in Python?", define what "strong" means. An unclear definition makes the probability hard to interpret. A value of 0.5 does not mean medium skill. Use a [Score](/primitives/score) to measure skill along defined levels. [Choose a question type](/primitives#choose-a-question-type) explains the distinction.

## Example questions

```
"Is the customer requesting a refund?"
"Does this resume mention experience with distributed systems?"
"Does the message contain personally identifiable information?"
"Does the room have a minifridge?"
```

## Tips and advanced usage

* **Phrasing.** Beyond a plain question, you can phrase the instruction as a statement for the model to evaluate for truthfulness. For "the customer is requesting a refund", a value near 1 means the statement is true. Try both phrasings with your own data to see what works best.
* **Optional `criteria`.** The instruction is enough for most Noul questions, but when the boundary between yes and no is subtle, pass `criteria` with `true` and `false` descriptions to pin down what each outcome means — as shown in the request example above.

# API reference

> Full HTTP API reference for the TypeSafe evaluation endpoint.

Evaluate a `state` against a map of typed `questions` and get back structured `answers`, one per question. For a guided introduction, start with the [primitives](/primitives).

## Evaluation endpoint

```http theme={null}
POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone
Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>
Content-Type: application/json
```

## Request body

The top-level shape of every request. Each entry in the `questions` map is a typed question you name.

<ParamField body="state" type="string | object | array" required>
  The content to evaluate. A plain string for text, or structured data (object/array) for things like chat logs, records, or the current state of your application. See [State](/concepts/state) for formats and best practices.
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="model" type="string" required>
  The model that handles the request. Use `"jev-latest"`, TypeSafe's flagship model. See [Models](/models) for the available models and aliases.
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="questions" type="map<string, Question>" required>
  A map of typed [Question](#question-types) objects. You choose each key; answers come back under the same keys.

  <Expandable title="map entries">
    <ParamField body="‹question id›" type="Question">
      A key you choose. The matching [Answer](#answer-types) is returned under this same id. The key is not sent to the underlying model and is not used in inference.
    </ParamField>
  </Expandable>
</ParamField>

```json Example request theme={null}
{
  "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days.",
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "questions": {
    "is_urgent": {
      "type": "noul",
      "instructions": "Does this convey urgency?"
    }
  }
}
```

## Question types

A `Question` is one of three types, set by its `type` field. All three share `type` and `instructions`; each adds its own `criteria`.

### Noul

A yes/no question. Returns the probability the answer is yes.

<ParamField body="type" type=""noul"" required />

<ParamField body="instructions" type="string | object | array" required>
  The yes/no question to evaluate.
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="criteria" type="object">
  Optional descriptions of what a yes and a no mean.

  <Expandable title="properties">
    <ParamField body="true" type="string">
      What a yes (value near 1) means.
    </ParamField>

    <ParamField body="false" type="string">
      What a no (value near 0) means.
    </ParamField>
  </Expandable>
</ParamField>

```json Example request focus={5-12} theme={null}
{
  "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days.",
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "questions": {
    "is_urgent": {
      "type": "noul",
      "instructions": "Does this convey urgency?",
      "criteria": {
        "true": "Explicitly time-sensitive",
        "false": "No urgency expressed"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### Choice

Picks one option from a set you define. Returns the chosen option and the full probability distribution.

<ParamField body="type" type=""choice"" required />

<ParamField body="instructions" type="string | object | array" required>
  What the model should decide.
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="criteria" type="map<string, string | null>" required>
  A map of option to rubric description; use null when an option needs no extra detail.

  <Expandable title="map entries">
    <ParamField body="‹option›" type="string | null">
      A key you choose. A description of this option.
    </ParamField>
  </Expandable>
</ParamField>

```json Example request focus={5-13} theme={null}
{
  "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days.",
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "questions": {
    "department": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
      "criteria": {
        "billing": "Payments, invoicing, refunds",
        "technical": "Bugs, outages, integrations",
        "sales": "Pricing, upgrades, new accounts"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### Score

Rates the state along a rubric you define. Returns a probability-weighted value across your levels.

<ParamField body="type" type=""score"" required />

<ParamField body="instructions" type="string | object | array" required>
